data.title: Sorry, congressman: Spending four days in Havana is not the same as knowing Cuba
data.description:
At a recent House Foreign Affairs hearing, Rep. Mark Pocan (D-Wisc.) told Ambassador Mike Waltz he would not take his advice on Cuba because Waltz had never been there. Pocan had returned days earlier from four days in Havana.

He is half right: Having been there matters. I was born in Cuba and raised there. In 1992, I left on a raft, eight hours to a boat and then several days crossing the Straits of Florida. The boat was sinking. There were sharks around it. Scholars estimate that at least one in four people who attempt that crossing never arrive.

But four days of government-arranged meetings is not the same as having been to Cuba, and neither is a family story. What decides whether you understand a country is who you were allowed to talk to.

Meeting President Miguel Díaz-Canel was not the mistake; you cannot change policy between two governments without talking to the other government. What they saw was real: Premature infants on ventilators that fail when the grid does. The problem is not that they met the government. It is that the government was the only party that got to describe the country to them.

Consider what happened in April, when an earlier delegation was on the island. Cuba’s government announced it was releasing 2,010 prisoners and called it a humanitarian gesture. Human Rights Watch, Prisoners Defenders, and Justicia 11J, which tracks cases from the July 2021 protests, went looking afterward. None could identify a single political prisoner among those freed. The government had said as much in its own announcement, which excluded anyone convicted of “crimes against authority,” the category Cuba has used for six decades to imprison people for what they said.

Two thousand people walked out of prison. Not one had been put there for speaking. Families in Cuba knew within a day; they were the ones at the gates.

My picture of Cuba is not a memory from 1992. For 20 years, I have mailed relatives what their hospitals lack: surgical instruments, needles and the thread to close the wound. But U.S. representatives were falsely told that this scarcity is recent.

Cuban authorities acknowledged chronic drug shortages in 2017 and named surgery among the worst-hit specialties in 2022. Since 2021. They have let travelers import medicine duty-free and without limit. The director of a Havana children’s hospital said this spring that Cuba has lived with this for decades and that it has now reached dramatic levels.

Both halves are true, but the delegation repeated only one.

None of that will settle the debate about sanctions. The claim I am making is narrower: A delegation that meets the president, the foreign minister and the national assembly has heard from one party to a dispute.

Estimates of Cuba’s political prisoner population run from roughly roughly 700 to more than 1,200, depending on who is counting, and there have been more than 175 new cases this year. Take the low estimate if you prefer. Seven hundred people is still 700 people, and not one of them or their families briefed the congressional delegation.

Members who travel to Cuba should request meetings in writing and in advance with families of imprisoned protesters, independent journalists and clergy operating outside state approval. They should then speak publicly when they are refused, since a refusal is itself information.

They should ask about named cases. Take, for example, the four teenagers arrested after blackout protests in Morón, in central Cuba. One is 15 years old, below Cuba’s own minimum age of criminal responsibility.

And members of Congress should publish their itineraries, showing who they met and who arranged it.

None of this requires anyone to change position on the embargo. It does require visitors to stop describing Cuba after speaking only with its government during brief visits.

I want the blackouts to end. I want my family to eat; I would take that from anyone willing to grant it.

What I cannot accept is the pretense that the Cuban state is the only Cuban voice with an address, and that the rest of us — the imprisoned, the drowned, and the ones who made it — are mere scenery.

Yenisel Cruz-Almeida is a professor at the University of Florida. She left Cuba by raft in 1992.

data.title: Rick Scott on Fauci contempt vote: 'All he had to do was tell the truth'
data.description:
Sen. Rick Scott (R-Fla.) stood by a vote to refer Anthony Fauci to be held in contempt of Congress, arguing the former chief White House medical adviser could have avoided the escalation by answering lawmakers’ questions about the COVID-19 pandemic.

“We were really disappointed. We wanted to just get facts last week,” Scott told The Hill’s Batya Ungar-Sargon late Thursday on “On Balance.” “He failed to give the answers and he could have. All he had to do was tell the truth. So he was held in contempt.”

The Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee voted 8-5 earlier Thursday to hold Fauci in contempt after the former official refused to answer a single question, invoking his Fifth Amendment right 111 times during his hostile Senate hearing last week.

Scott, who sits on the committee, said that Republicans had hoped to get answers from Fauci about questions that have persisted since the pandemic, including the origins of COVID-19, vaccines and the government’s handling of the crisis.

Scott pointed to Fauci’s sweeping pardon, which was granted to him by former President Biden and covers conduct from January, 2014 through January, 2025. 

Scott said questions surrounding the government’s pandemic response continue to have consequences years later, pointing to Americans who remain uncertain about vaccines and a heightened distrust in the American public health care system.

“Why did he tell us to shut down our government? So many businesses shut down because of his actions. Why did he lie to us about the medicines, the vaccine? Why did he change everything?” Scott asked. “There’s so many people, my daughters with kids are saying, do I give my kids vaccines or not?”

The Florida Republican urged the Justice Department to take the contempt matter seriously. The contempt resolution, brought by committee Chair Rand Paul (R-Ky.), was referred to the Justice Department for potential prosecution.

“I hope they look at it seriously and hold him accountable for his lies,” Scott said.

data.title: Talarico opens 4-point lead over Paxton in Texas Senate poll
data.description:
Texas state Rep. James Talarico (D) has a 4-point lead over state Attorney General Ken Paxton (R) in the Lone Star State’s Senate race, according to a new survey.

The Texas Pulse/Texas A&M Bush School poll, released Friday, shows 47 percent of likely Texas voters plan to support Talarico while 43 percent chose Paxton. In the group’s June survey, the two candidates were tied at 46 percent.

“The movement over the last two months is largely seen by looking at independent voters who now favor Talarico by 23 points,” ReconMR Senior Research Analyst Lindsey Hendren, who was cited in the latest survey, said.

Among independents, Talarico leads Paxton 53 percent to 30 percent, the poll found.

The poll offers an encouraging sign for Democrats as they look to make inroads in Texas, where Republicans have dominated statewide elections for decades.

Women favor Talarico over Paxton with 53 percent support to the attorney general’s 40 percent. On the other side, the state’s top prosecutor leads the lawmaker among men with 47 percent to 41 percent, respectively, according to the numbers.

Talarico also holds sizable support from younger voters, with 66 percent of those aged 18 to 34 backing the Democrat compared with 23 percent for the GOP candidate, who was backed by President Trump.

Support for the candidates is also widely based on geography, underscoring the state’s political divide.

“Talarico leads by wide margins in the Austin and Dallas/Ft. Worth regions, while Paxton has a large lead in the rural parts of the state, and the Houston and San Antonio regions are currently very closely divided,” Hendren said.

Talarico also outperformed Paxton on most of the issues tested in the poll. Voters favored the Democrat over Republican on affordability, keeping Texans safe and managing the state’s water supply. 

The only issue Paxton had a slight advantage was securing the southern border with Mexico. Voters also viewed the attorney general as tougher than Talarico, but also more corrupt, according to the analysis.

“The good news for Talarico is that voters think he is honest, authentic, in touch with Texas values, and that he’s not corrupt,” said Veteran pollster and Texas A&M Visiting Professor Clifford Young. “The bad news for him is that voters by a narrow margin don’t think he’s tough.”

“For Paxton, the good news is voters think he’s tough. But the bad news is that a majority or plurality of voters say that Paxton is not honest, authentic, or in touch with Texas values,” Young continued. “And even worse, by a 55-35% margin, voters say Paxton is corrupt.”

The survey was conducted July 27-30 among 619 likely Texas voters, using a combination of landline, cellphone and text-to-web responses. The overall margin of error was plus or minus 4.7 percentage points.

data.title: Trump: It's a 'mistake' to go against data centers
data.description:
President Trump touted what he said were the benefits of data centers in an interview that was published on Friday, potentially pitting himself against a number of Republicans and Democrats on the growing issue.

“I saw Texas the other day sort of against data centers. I think it’s a mistake,” Trump told Punchbowl News.

“I’m not taking positions,” he continued. “I just think it’s a mistake because there are other communities that want it. When a community wants it, it means a lot of money is going to come into that community.”

The president appeared to be referring to a move from Texas Gov. Greg Abbott (R ) on Monday to place a moratorium on data centers until regulatory agencies complete their audit on the centers.

“Our top priority is to protect Texans’ safety and quality of life,” Abbott said in a statement at the time. “Any project that fails to comply with the requirements set forth by the PUCT and ERCOT, and by state law, must be denied connection to the Texas grid. Simply put, Texans must come first.”

However, Trump said in the new interview that, if he were a governor, he “would want data centers so badly.”

“Taxes are going to go way down because this is a tremendous source of income,” the president said

Trump also pushed back on criticism of the data centers, including that they’re unsightly.

“I don’t think they’re unsightly. I mean, I’m looking at some of these data centers, the most incredible buildings I’ve ever seen,” the president said.

“They are tremendously important for the economics. I mean, this is—for Texas to say no to data centers is a mistake in the sense that it could be bigger than oil,” he said.

Trump also warned against pushing back against data centers, arguing the U.S. cannot let China “beat us” on the issue.

“We can’t let China beat us at this. You know, a lot of people think that the campaign that’s being put on is being paid for by China.”

Trump also said he will speak to Chinese President Xi Jinping about data centers during a state visit in September.

“But I don’t blame him. I mean, we do things and they do things,” he said.

Reuters reported earlier this week that the Trump administration was planning to ban Chinese imports of optical transceivers from data centers by the end of the year.

data.title: HHS should protect payments to clinical trial participants
data.description:
In 2002, San Francisco voters passed the “Care Not Cash” measure, built on a simple intuition: Stop handing cash to homeless people, because they will only waste it on drugs and alcohol.

By then, we were a decade into doing the opposite — paying people who used drugs, often hundreds of dollars at a time, to take part in research. The conventional wisdom said we were funding relapse, but it was wrong. When researchers have looked, the bulk of the money goes to rent, food, and bills, not drugs.

New treatments get developed only when the people who need them can afford the time, travel, and support to take part. The studies we were working to complete tested the buprenorphine and naloxone combination now sold as Suboxone, in people actively using heroin.

The federal government is now asking the same question we spent years answering. As part of a broader effort to support American clinical research, the HHS Office of Inspector General has opened a formal request for comment on whether to protect payments to clinical trial participants, with comments due Aug. 24.

For decades, those payments have sat in a legal gray zone, created by an anti-kickback statute and a related rule that penalizes offering inducements to Medicare and Medicaid patients. The worry is that reimbursing a federal beneficiary’s costs can look like an inducement to use reimbursable services, even when those costs would have been incurred in routine care anyway. The bioethics worry is that money could corrupt the choices of vulnerable people.

That bioethics concern has been tested in people who use drugs, where the fear that cash buys drugs and addiction clouds consent is sharpest. In randomized studies, paying people who use drugs, even substantial amounts in cash, did not raise their drug use or make them feel coerced, and improved follow-up.

Asked whether research money pulls them into studies they would otherwise refuse, participants tend to reject the premise. They can get drugs without it. There is even evidence that payment helps: In experimental studies, higher payments make participants more attentive to risk disclosures, not less, treating a larger offer as a signal of higher stakes.

A rigorous test came in 2021, when a study embedded randomized cash incentives inside two clinical trials. Incentives raised enrollment in one and made no difference in the other. In neither did they distort how people weighed the risks or skew the sample toward poorer participants.

Justice and scientific validity point the same way. The treatments that will work for people who use drugs, who are poor, or who are on Medicaid are the ones whose trials included them. Suboxone exists because we and other researchers were willing to study people who were actively using opioids instead of deciding they were too compromised to include. Refusing to pay the participants who can least afford to take part shifts the cost of research onto the people it is meant to serve, and builds the evidence base on people unlike them. The rules try to prevent exploitation from overpaying participants. They produce an exploitation in the other direction, underpaying or excluding the people who most need the answers.

The inspector general should codify two things. One is reimbursement for real out-of-pocket costs, which restores participants financially and should be uncontroversial. In 2018, FDA clarified that reimbursing travel and lodging does not raise undue-influence concerns; the inspector general should follow suit.

The other is compensation for time, which is more complex and should be left to the institutional review board. Hard dollar caps would be a mistake: the right compensation depends on what a study asks of people. A cap low enough to feel safe to regulators will either constrain protocols or shut out the people research needs. Protections should also reach beyond government-sponsored trials to the academic and industry trials where most research happens. Review boards already weigh whether participants are fairly paid and protected, and should keep doing so.

Care Not Cash drew on the conviction that some people cannot be trusted with money. The clinical trials showed the opposite. They also showed that the buprenorphine-naloxone combination behaved as hoped in the people who would actually need it. Suboxone has since saved many lives. None of that would have happened without people who were actively using opioids taking part in those trials.

And Care Not Cash governed welfare, not work. Clinical trial participation is work. It means showing up on time, following protocol, and sometimes accepting real physical risk. Medicaid now has work requirements of its own, and the work that helps cure the diseases that trap people in poverty should count. The inspector general can write that lesson into the rules, or write in the old fear instead. It should choose the evidence.

Matthew Baggott, PhD, is a neuroscientist and CEO of Tactogen Inc. John Mendelson, MD, is a board-certified internist with over 30 years in the field of addiction treatment, and is Chief Medical Officer and Founder of Ria Health.

data.title: Live updates: Senate faces day of big votes with Blanche's nomination on the ropes
data.description:
The Senate is scrambling to leave for its August recess but has several hurdles to jump before it gets there after a week of infighting.

The biggest items on the list include acting Attorney General Todd Blanche’s nomination for the permanent job. On Friday morning, Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska) announced she was a “no” vote, leaving Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) little room to maneuver. If Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-La.) also becomes a “no,” the nomination may need to be put on ice.

Starting with a morning vote series, the upper chamber will try to pass a Russia sanctions bill championed by the late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.) and a bloc of nominees. It will also vote on college sports legislation and a continuing resolution to fund the government into December.

President Trump on Friday has policy meetings at the White House and a roundtable at the State Department, before heading to Bedminster, N.J.

Follow live here.

data.title: US loses 23k jobs in July, unemployment dips slightly
data.description:
The U.S. economy lost 23,000 jobs in July, and the unemployment rate dipped slightly to 4.1 percent, according to new data released Friday by the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS). 

Economists had expected American employers to add 83,000 jobs and the jobless rate to hold steady at 4.2 percent last month, according to consensus estimates. 

This comes on the heels of relatively weak jobs numbers in June, in which the U.S. workforce initially saw just 57,000 new roles added, well below the 110,000 that experts anticipated.  

Both the May and June jobs reports, however, were revised lower Friday by a combined 103,000. The updated numbers now show employers adding just 20,000 jobs last month, while the prior month’s job gains were reduced from 129,000 to 63,000.

President Trump and Republican lawmakers are grappling with persistent inflation and a relatively sluggish economy just three months out from the midterm elections, in which affordability has become a central issue. 

Annual inflation dipped slightly to 3.7 percent in June, according to the personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index, the Federal Reserve’s preferred measure of inflation.  

This was down from a three-year high of 4.1 percent in May, as a brief ceasefire with Iran eased energy prices on hopes that ships would begin transporting more oil through the Strait of Hormuz. 

It’s unclear whether inflation will continue to trend downward, after Washington and Tehran began trading strikes again in early July. However, hostilities eased in recent days, as Iran and Oman have negotiated over a potential deal to reopen the key waterway. 

Meanwhile, the economy showed signs of slowing in the second quarter, with U.S. gross domestic product (GDP) increasing at an annual rate of 1.5 percent, down from 2.1 percent in the prior three-month period. 

The Fed, which met in mid-July, opted to hold interest rates steady in a split 9-3 decision. It marked the fifth straight time the rate-setting panel has voted to keep rates at their current level, even as Trump has put pressure on new Fed Chair Kevin Warsh to cut rates. 

Following the meeting, Warsh touted the economy’s “impressive resilience” in the face of “recent shocks,” while maintaining that the central bank is “resolute” in bringing inflation down to the Fed’s target rate of 2 percent.

data.title: Crenshaw weighs in on 'dumb' $20 burrito sparking debate over affordability
data.description:
Rep. Dan Crenshaw (R-Texas) doubled down on his comments Thursday after drawing criticism for telling Americans concerned about high food prices to “stop whining” and “get a job,” as a viral debate over the cost of a $20 burrito exposed divisions among the GOP over affordability.

“Just hearing about this dumb $20 burrito debate so just thought I’d make the losers on social media angry before going to bed,” Crenshaw posted on social platform X late Wednesday.

“Stop whining, get a job, eat Ramen like the rest of us did in college, on a budget with 4 roommates,” he wrote. “The market doesn’t care what you think something ‘should’ cost.”

After taking some heat in his comment section, the lawmaker sent out another post to address the backlash before doubling down on his previous remarks.

“Okay, I am SORRY for triggering the comment section,” Crenshaw wrote on X. 

The Texas Republican then sarcastically suggested the existence of a $20 burrito was proof capitalism had failed before making it clear he was joking.

“Remember when the right had principles and made fun of leftists for elevating victimhood as a virtue? Want to tell people the truth? Or just bribe them for their vote in the next election?” he wrote.

Crenshaw, who recently lost his bid for reelection, had ironically criticized the Biden administration in 2021 after it told Americans to eat less take-out beef and poultry to mediate inflation.

“America: our food prices are too high what are you doing about inflation? Biden admin: just be vegan and stop complaining you bunch of rubes,” he said in his 2021 post.

The burrito debate began earlier this week, after Turning Point USA spokesperson Andrew Kolvet shared a conversation with a college student who summed up his concerns about affordability by saying, “A burrito shouldn’t cost $20.”

“A lot of this is a hangover from Covid and Biden-era inflation, but the lived experience is the same: It just feels like basic things cost too much,” Kolvet wrote online.

Vice President Vance also weighed in on the discussion, after Washington Post columnist and Fox News contributor Marc Thiessen dismissed Kolvet’s complaint.

“Cry me a river. The burritos in the college cafeteria are included in your meal plan,” Thiessen wrote.

Vance replied to Thiessen with a jab about his weight.

“I’m surprised to hear Mark say this,” Vance wrote on X. “If you’ve ever met him in person, it’s quite obvious the man has never missed a burrito.”

Kolvet later told NewsNation’s “On Balance” that he “had no idea” that his comments would spur such a debate, but that it would be a mistake for the GOP to repeat the mistakes of former President Biden by dismissing the concern about food prices.

“I think it’s political malfeasance to ignore and deny the actual anxieties of voters, especially young voters,” he said.

data.title: Section 31 tariffs are meant to be a scalpel, not a sledgehammer
data.description:
Congress never intended for Section 301 of the 1974 Trade Act to be a general tariff statute. It wrote the statute as a targeted trade remedy. That distinction matters. In fact, it’s at the heart of the latest lawsuit challenging the Trump administration’s Section 301 tariffs.  

The case, brought by the Liberty Justice Center, nominally concerns tariffs on imports from 60 economies for their alleged failures to combat forced labor. But the bigger question is whether Section 301 remains a targeted trade remedy, or whether it’s been transformed into a general source of presidential tariff authority?

The statute itself provides the answer. 

Section 301 establishes a clear statutory chain. The U.S. Trade Representative must identify a particular foreign “act, policy, or practice,” determine that it burdens or restricts U.S. commerce and explain why the chosen response is an “appropriate and feasible” means of securing the elimination of the practice. 

That sequence is not a procedural formality. It is the statute’s limiting principle. 

Congress designed Section 301 as targeted economic diplomacy. Tariffs are not the objective; they are the instrument. Their purpose is to induce a foreign government to abandon a particular practice.

The stronger the connection between the identified practice and the chosen remedy, the more faithfully the executive is carrying out Congress’s design. The latest litigation argues that the connection has broken down. 

No one disputes that forced labor is a grave human rights abuse. The question before the court of International Trade is whether nearly uniform tariffs imposed on substantially all imports from 60 economies are an “appropriate and feasible” means of persuading each of those governments to strengthen enforcement against forced labor. 

That is precisely the inquiry Congress required. If the executive no longer must demonstrate how a tariff is likely to eliminate the specific foreign practice it identifies, then Section 301 ceases to function as Congress intended. It becomes something much broader: authority to impose tariffs whenever the executive concludes that another country’s policies deserve economic pressure. 

That’s not what Congress enacted. The broader structure of American trade law confirms the point. 

Congress has never delegated tariff authority through a single all-purpose statute. Instead, it created specialized authorities for specialized problems. Section 232 addresses national security, for example, and Section 122 authorizes temporary, across the board tariffs during balance of payments crises. Section 301 occupies a very different role by authorizing targeted responses to specific foreign trade practices. 

The distinctions are deliberate. Congress wanted different legal standards to govern different exercises of presidential power. 

Section 122 illustrates why that matters. Congress anticipated that presidents might seek broad tariffs affecting virtually the entire economy. It granted that authority but imposed strict limits. Under this statute, tariffs can’t exceed 15 percent and can only remain in effect for a maximum of 150 days without congressional approval. 

Those restrictions reflect a legislative judgment that economy-wide tariff authority should be temporary and politically accountable. Yet, if Section 301 can be interpreted to sustain substantially similar tariff programs indefinitely, those limits lose their force. A statute Congress designed for targeted trade retaliation starts performing the work Congress assigned elsewhere under much tighter constraints. 

Courts ordinarily reject interpretations that produce that result. One of the oldest principles of statutory interpretation is that Congress does not legislate redundantly. Statutes should complement one another, not allow one delegation to swallow the rest. That principle should guide the Court of International Trade here.

This case is not ultimately about whether tariffs are good policy or whether forced labor deserves a forceful response. It’s about whether courts will preserve the statutory limits Congress placed on one of its most consequential delegations of economic authority. 

Congress did not delegate a general power to impose tariffs whenever the executive identifies an international problem worthy of economic pressure. It authorized a far narrower authority: identify a specific foreign act, policy or practice, determine that it burdens U.S. commerce and justify the chosen tariff as an appropriate and feasible means of eliminating that practice. 

That statutory chain is not a technicality. It is what distinguishes Section 301 from a general tariff law. 

If courts allow that chain to be broken, Section 301 will no longer be a targeted trade remedy. It will become the executive branch’s default source of tariff authority whenever other statutes prove unavailable or inconvenient. That would do more than expand Section 301. It would erase one of the principal limits that Congress placed on the executive’s authority to impose tariffs. 

Section 301 was written to be a scalpel. Courts should not allow it to become a sledgehammer. 

Marc L. Busch is the Karl F. Landegger Professor of International Business Diplomacy at the Walsh School of Foreign Service, Georgetown University. Petros Mavroidis is the Edwin B. Parker Professor of Foreign and Comparative Law at Columbia Law School.

data.title: Trump declines to back Thune for another term as Senate GOP leader
data.description:
President Trump declined to back Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-N.D.) for a second term as Republican leader in the chamber, saying he did not want to discuss the matter, in an interview that aired on Friday. 

“I don’t want to get into that necessarily,” Trump told Punchbowl News. 

“I get along with him. It’s unfortunate that he doesn’t have the votes,” he said, referring to Thune insisting Senate Republicans do not have the votes to pass the Safeguard American Voter Eligibility (SAVE America) Act. 

When pressed on whether he gets along with Thune, Trump said, “I do,” but noted he has disagreements with the Senate leader. 

“I believe strongly in terminating the filibuster, and by the way, getting SAVE America Act approved immediately, and about 400 other things in every hour of every day,” the president said. 

Thune has repeatedly said Senate Republicans do not have the votes to pass the SAVE America Act and has thrown cold water on the prospect of eliminating the filibuster. The topic has become a point of contention between them. 

Trump warned that Democrats would move to eliminate the filibuster if they take back control of the chamber because they would be able to pass legislation with a simple majority. 

“If they get in, they’re going to do it very quickly,” the president said. “I would do whether they did it or not. We would get in the next two and a half years, we would get things that nobody ever dreamt of. We would be in office for the next hundred years.” 

“And I tell you what, if they get it in, I will be the last Republican president,” he said.
